differences.title: 1. EXECUTION MODEL
differences.leftDesc: llama.cpp loads GGUF models and runs a tight inference loop (token-by-token or batched internally) optimized for small, local deployments. It heavily relies on quantized weight layouts and CPU kernels.
differences.rightDesc: vLLM builds a high-throughput serving runtime around paged attention and a scheduler. It keeps the model resident and multiplexes many concurrent decode requests efficiently across GPU SMs.

differences.title: 2. BATCHING STRATEGY
differences.leftDesc: llama.cpp generally batches at the granularity supported by its backend, often focusing on single-user latency. It may use simple batching for throughput, but it doesn’t orchestrate decode-time interleaving like large GPU serving stacks.
differences.rightDesc: vLLM performs continuous batching by admitting new requests during decode and interleaving token generation across requests. This reduces idle GPU time and boosts tokens/sec while keeping latency predictable.

differences.title: 3. ATTENTION MEMORY
differences.leftDesc: In llama.cpp, KV cache management is tied to its inference loop and backend-specific implementations, optimized for host RAM or device buffers depending on build. Quantization reduces memory pressure for activations.
differences.rightDesc: vLLM uses a paged KV cache (block-based allocation) so sequences grow without reallocating large contiguous buffers. This prevents fragmentation and allows dynamic request admission at scale.

differences.title: 4. QUANTIZATION ECOSYSTEM
differences.leftDesc: llama.cpp’s production strength is its broad support for GGUF quantization formats (e.g., Q4/Q5/Q8 families) and corresponding CPU/GPU kernels. It trades some quality for speed and memory fit on limited hardware.
differences.rightDesc: vLLM focuses on efficient inference for higher-performance deployment, using quantization support aligned with its GPU kernels and runtime scheduling. KV cache handling and kernel choices drive practical memory/latency outcomes.

differences.title: 5. DEPLOYMENT SHAPE
differences.leftDesc: llama.cpp is commonly deployed as a local binary or embedded library, making it ideal for edge devices, developer laptops, or constrained servers. Scaling usually means running multiple replicas behind a load balancer.
differences.rightDesc: vLLM is designed for production serving with an API process managing GPU resources, scheduling, and request lifecycles. It fits naturally into multi-instance GPU fleets with autoscaling and metrics pipelines.

differences.title: 6. LATENCY BEHAVIOR
differences.leftDesc: With llama.cpp, latency is often dominated by CPU compute or a specific offload backend, and there’s less complex queueing. For one request, performance is straightforward to reason about.
differences.rightDesc: vLLM must manage queueing across many concurrent decodes. Its scheduler targets minimizing stalls by prioritizing active sequences, balancing throughput with mechanisms to reduce tail latency under load.

differences.title: 7. HARDWARE UTILIZATION
differences.leftDesc: llama.cpp supports CPU execution and optional GPU/offload backends depending on build options. It maximizes usefulness per watt by leveraging quantized math and tailored kernels to fit consumer hardware constraints.
differences.rightDesc: vLLM is built to saturate GPUs for large-batch decode. It keeps compute busy by overlapping scheduling decisions with GPU execution and by using memory-efficient attention/KV handling to reduce bandwidth bottlenecks.
